How should the Moderate phase be assessed?

The significance of Moderate nationalism cannot be measured only by the number of reforms immediately granted by the British government.

The early nationalists worked during a period when political awareness was still developing and the Congress had a relatively narrow social base. Their activities helped establish important ideas, methods and organisations that supported the subsequent expansion of the national movement.

At the same time, their reliance on constitutional appeals and limited public participation restricted their immediate political influence.

Major achievements of the Moderates

Creation of an all-India political organisation

The Indian National Congress provided a common platform through which political leaders from different regions could meet regularly and discuss national concerns.

Before its establishment, political activity had largely been organised through provincial associations. Congress sessions helped connect these separate activities and encouraged cooperation across regional boundaries.

This organisational achievement was important even though the Congress initially represented only a relatively small educated section of Indian society.

Development of national political consciousness

The Moderates argued that important economic, administrative and political grievances were shared by Indians across regions and communities.

They encouraged people to consider government policies from an Indian national perspective rather than only through local or provincial interests.

Through speeches, newspapers, meetings and Congress resolutions, they helped establish public discussion of national political questions.

Political education and constitutional awareness

The Moderate leaders explained concepts such as representation, legislative accountability, public expenditure and civil rights.

They also familiarised politically active Indians with the use of resolutions, petitions and public debate.

These methods helped develop organisational skills and political awareness that continued to be useful as the nationalist movement expanded.

Exposure of economic exploitation

The economic arguments of Dadabhai Naoroji, Romesh Chandra Dutt and other nationalist thinkers helped explain how colonial policies could affect India's economic development.

They connected questions of poverty, taxation, industrial decline and public expenditure with the political structure of colonial rule.

This economic critique provided a powerful argument for greater Indian control over government decisions.

Limited constitutional concessions

The Indian Councils Act of 1892 introduced a limited expansion of legislative participation and permitted restricted budget discussion and administrative questions.

These changes were broadly related to demands advanced by early nationalists, although they did not satisfy the Congress's expectations.

The Act should not be treated as proof that the Moderates had secured representative self-government. Colonial officials continued to retain decisive authority.

Major limitations of the Moderate phase

A narrow social base

The early Congress was dominated by educated professionals and influential urban public figures.

Peasants, agricultural labourers, industrial workers, women and many disadvantaged social groups did not participate in comparable numbers.

Consequently, although Congress leaders claimed to speak for Indian interests generally, their organisation had not yet developed extensive participation among the wider population.

Dependence on British willingness to reform

The Moderates generally believed that constitutional arguments and appeals to British political principles could persuade the colonial government to introduce reforms.

However, British authorities did not consistently accept nationalist demands, particularly when those demands challenged established political and administrative control.

Reliance on persuasion therefore restricted the effectiveness of Moderate politics when the government refused to cooperate.

Limited immediate political results

Many Moderate demands were repeated over several years without being implemented fully.

Legislative reforms remained restricted, senior administrative positions continued to be dominated by Europeans, and Indians did not obtain effective control over the colonial executive.

The Congress could express criticism and organise public pressure, but it could not compel the government to accept its resolutions.

Absence of a broad mass movement

Moderate political activity relied heavily on annual meetings, newspaper campaigns, constitutional petitions and educated leadership.

These methods were useful for developing public awareness, but they did not immediately produce sustained nationwide participation among ordinary people.

Later nationalist leaders increasingly argued that political change required wider mobilisation and methods that placed greater pressure on colonial authority.

Why did criticism of Moderate politics grow?

By the late 19th century, some nationalist leaders were dissatisfied with the slow progress of constitutional reforms.

They argued that repeatedly asking the colonial government for concessions could not by itself secure meaningful political power.

Leaders such as Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal and Lala Lajpat Rai became associated with more assertive political ideas and criticised excessive reliance on petitions.

The development of these differences marked a transition in nationalist politics. However, the rise of more assertive approaches did not erase the organisational and intellectual contributions made during the Moderate phase.

Important distinctions for understanding the period

ConceptCorrect understandingCommon confusion
Pre-Congress associationsRegional and other political bodies established before 1885All were branches of the Congress
Congress foundationEstablishment of a national political organisation in 1885Beginning of mass participation by all sections of society
Moderate nationalismPolitical reform through constitutional methodsComplete absence of opposition to colonial policies
Drain of wealthTransfer of resources abroad without equivalent returnEvery export from India was an economic drain

Historical significance

The Moderate phase represented an important stage in the development of organised Indian nationalism.

The early political associations established experience in constitutional representation. The Congress brought leaders from different regions onto a common platform. Moderate nationalists developed shared political demands and systematically criticised the economic effects of colonial rule.

Their immediate political achievements were limited, but they helped create the institutional and intellectual foundations on which later nationalist activity developed.

The central distinction is that the Moderates were more successful in developing organised political nationalism than in obtaining immediate control over colonial government.

The early national movement at a glance

Prelims focus

  • Early political associations prepared the organisational ground for the Congress.
  • Indian National Congress: established in 1885.
  • Moderate phase: commonly dated 1885–1905.
  • Principal Moderate methods: petitions, resolutions, public meetings and constitutional appeals.
  • Economic critique: Dadabhai Naoroji's Drain of Wealth Theory and R. C. Dutt's criticism of colonial economic policies.
  • Indian Councils Act, 1892: limited constitutional reforms, not responsible government.
  • Trap: The limited immediate success of the Moderates does not mean they made no contribution to Indian nationalism.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 9, The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947, printed pp. 110–113, 2020–21 edition; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, Chapter 1, sections 1.2–1.5; Drishti IAS, To What Extent Did the Role of the Moderates Prepare a Base for the Wider Freedom Movement?, 17 January 2022; Drishti IAS, Examine the Significance of the Era of Moderates in the Indian National Congress, 28 December 2024; President of India, History of Parliamentary Democracy in India, paragraphs 19–22 concerning the Indian Councils Act of 1892, consulted 20 November 2026.]

title: Achievements, Limitations and Historical Importance of Moderate Nationalism
